name: Pressure washing and window cleaning
summary: Start a pressure washing and window cleaning business: your first 25 people and partners, a price menu by house size from real ranges, quotes with measured surfaces and a storefront route.
door_hello: Your house, washed clean, no ladder work for you
door_step3: I wash it with low pressure and send photos

promises.offer: Your price menu by house size, the first-clients ladder, a storefront route and job math, on a one-page offer sheet.

promises.reply: Paste what someone wrote back: what they meant, a short answer with one next step, and your Pipeline updated. A draft you send yourself.
promises.won: Log the yes, then everything for the job: the booking text, a prep text, a printable job sheet, the after-job text and the invoice.
promises.proof: One wash turned into proof: a result card, a before-and-after collage from your photos, a caption, an honest review ask and a case study once they say yes.
promises.next_25: The next 25 painters, agents, managers and restaurants near you that are not in your Pipeline yet, each with its messages, saved for Do my day.
promises.ready: Look ready before you reach out: a one-page website, a Google profile kit and a flyer, all from your real prices.
promises.storefronts: Shops and cafes near you in walking order, with a free demo window, a counter script, a rate sheet and directions for each leg.
promises.season_plan: Twelve months of offers for where you live: what to sell each month, who to reach, what to presell, with a calendar file and a one-page plan.

off_season.play: Book spring house washes with a deposit, run a storefront window route, and sell holiday light installs.

licenses.disclaimer: General information, not legal advice. Rules differ by state, county and city: check your state and city.

items.what_to_check: Most areas need only a city or county business license; some cities want contractor registration for commercial work.

sources.says: Licenses and permits depend on business activity and location; local governments set registration, licensing and permitting rules; research your own state, county and city; some licenses expire and must be renewed.
Most areas require a business license only; some cities require contractor licenses for commercial work; check local rules for water runoff and environmental permits.

items.what_to_check: Cities must ban non-stormwater discharges to storm drains, so keep wash water and chemicals out of drains and ask your city stormwater office what it requires (blocking, recovery or permits).

sources.says: Small municipal storm sewer permits must require the city to effectively prohibit, through ordinance or other regulatory mechanism, non-storm water discharges into the storm sewer system and to enforce it.
Do not discharge wash water containing chemicals or oils into storm drains; many municipalities require wastewater discharge permits and water reclamation systems.
Some regions require environmental permits due to water usage and runoff.

items.what_to_check: A product meant to kill or control a pest can be a regulated pesticide; ask your state pesticide agency whether applying it for pay needs an applicator license.

sources.says: A pesticide is any substance or mixture of substances intended for preventing, destroying, repelling, or mitigating any pest; it generally must be registered by EPA before sale.
If the business applies sealants or specific chemical treatments, the state may require a specialized contractor or pesticide applicator license.

items.what_to_check: If a job disturbs paint on a pre-1978 home, such as stripping or prep for repainting, EPA's lead RRP rule can apply and requires firm certification. Do not take paint-stripping jobs on older homes without checking.

sources.says: Anyone paid to perform work that disturbs paint in housing and child-occupied facilities built before 1978 must be certified, including sole proprietorships; covered activities include painting preparation; minor work disturbing 20 square feet or less of exterior paint is excluded.

items.item: Liability, commercial auto and workers comp
items.what_to_check: General liability covers damage to client property; commercial clients often ask for $1M to $2M coverage; workers comp once you hire.

sources.says: Lists common policies: general liability, product liability, professional liability, commercial property, home-based business insurance, and workers compensation; buy insurance required by law first, and taxes on employment insurance and workers compensation vary by state.
General liability $500 to $2,000 a year is essential; many commercial clients require $1M to $2M coverage; add workers comp when hiring.

items.what_to_check: OSHA fall rules bind employers; once you hire, they apply to your crew. High-rise window work can need rope-descent training and city permits.

sources.says: Falls are among the most common causes of serious work related injuries and deaths. OSHA requires employers to provide fall protection at elevations of four feet in general industry and six feet in construction.
Some cities add rules for commercial or multi-story work, like permits or documentation for rope descent systems, anchorage points, or OSHA fall protection compliance.

items.item: Chemical labels and safety data sheets
items.what_to_check: Keep the label and safety data sheet for each chemical (such as sodium hypochlorite) on the truck; employers must train workers on them.

sources.says: Hazard Communication standard (29 CFR 1910.1200): employers whose workers use hazardous chemicals need labels, safety data sheets and training.
Get an EIN directly from the IRS online in minutes for free.

steps: Quote: address, square footage or stories, surfaces (siding type, concrete, wood), photos of stains, mildew or oil; outdoor spigot location; pets and parked cars; year built if paint looks old.

Final walkthrough, after photos from the same angles, payment, review request, and offer the next visit (gutters in fall, windows every season).

objections.objection: I can rent a pressure washer and do it myself.
objections.answer: Rental plus a full weekend, plus the risk of streaks, etched concrete or stripped paint; you bring the right chemicals and finish in hours.

sources.says: Renting a pressure washer costs $40 to $100 daily (Consumer Reports); DIY jobs tend to take 10 times as long (pro quote); wrong pressure or chemicals can damage siding.

objections.say: You can! A rental takes most of a day, and the wrong pressure can etch concrete or strip paint. I bring the right equipment and cleaners. If you'd like, I'll do a small test spot first so you can see the difference.

objections.objection: Will it damage my siding, paint or plants?
objections.answer: Soft wash for siding and painted surfaces, low pressure, plants wetted first, and you are insured.

sources.says: Pressure washing may be too powerful for some surfaces such as painted siding; soft washing is reserved for safely cleaning vertical surfaces.

objections.say: I soft wash siding and painted surfaces at low pressure, I wet your plants before and after, and I take before photos of everything first. I carry insurance through [your insurer].

objections.answer: Do not match it; ask what it includes (screens, tracks, inside glass, sidewalks) and compare like for like.

sources.says: If a customer mentions a lower quote, don't match it; explain what's different. An $80 quote and a $280 quote often aren't for the same job.

objections.say: Could be a good deal! Before you decide, check what it includes: screens, tracks, sidewalks, downspouts? I'm happy to change what's in mine instead of cutting corners.

objections.objection: Why is there a minimum charge?
objections.answer: Travel, setup and teardown are the same for a small job; offer to add a second surface to reach the minimum.

sources.says: A minimum service fee covers travel, setup, prep and teardown; without one, small jobs become unprofitable.

objections.say: Travel and setup take the same time for a small job as a big one, so I have a minimum. We can add a second surface, like the front walk, so you get more for the same visit.

objections.answer: Say yes up front and name the spigot you need; most companies do.

sources.says: Some companies have their own water storage, but most use the home's water supply.

objections.say: Yes, I'll need an outdoor spigot that works. If yours is off for the winter, tell me and we'll plan around it.

objections.objection: Are you insured if something breaks?
objections.answer: Show the certificate before the job; commercial clients will ask for it.

sources.says: Confirm the pro has liability insurance and coverage in case of accidents during the job.

objections.say: Yes. I carry liability insurance through [your insurer], and I'll send the certificate before the job.

seasonality.pattern: Peak from March to June, steady in summer, a second peak in fall with gutter cleaning, and slow winters in cold climates. Southern states can work year round.

sources.says: Peak season March to June (book 4 to 6 weeks out); summer steady; fall second peak before holidays with gutter cleaning upsells; winter slow in cold climates; Texas, Florida and California year-round; Ohio 7 to 8 months.

seasonality.pattern: Mild spring and fall days are best for washing; companies run discounts in winter or early spring to fill schedules.

sources.says: Mild days in spring or fall are ideal for power washing; direct summer sun can dry the cleaning agent before rinsing; look for offers in slower seasons such as winter or early spring.

seasonality.pattern: Gutters are cleaned once or twice a year: in spring, and after fall leaves drop.

sources.says: Clean gutters twice a year: once in the spring and once after fall right into winter.

seasonality.pattern: Seasonal business: busy spring and summer, slow when it gets cold.

need: A day and time before you open, or a quiet hour
An outdoor spigot or a bucket of water from inside, only if the glass is very dirty
A contact who can tell me if anything changes
